dmm-2006-team-02.title: One pass at a time
dmm-2006-team-02.body:
In each pass the ball goes from one player to the other player's future position. Let the pass take $t$ seconds. Sideways the ball covers $100$ ft; lengthwise it covers $30t$ ft (the receiver is level with the passer when the ball is thrown and runs $30t$ ft before catching it); the ball's path has length $50t$:
$$(50t)^2=100^2+(30t)^2\ \Rightarrow\ 40t=100\ \Rightarrow\ t=2.5\text{ s}.$$
So each pass is $50\cdot2.5=125$ ft long and advances $75$ ft along the field. To cover $300$ ft takes $4$ passes: $4\cdot125=500$ ft.

**Answer: 500 feet**

dmm-2006-team-03.title: Pythagoras on the slanted side
dmm-2006-team-03.body:
Let $AD=h$, $CD=c$. Dropping a perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$ gives a right triangle with legs $h$ and $|26-c|$ and hypotenuse $BC=26+h$:
$$h^2+(26-c)^2=(26+h)^2\Rightarrow 676-52c+c^2=676+52h\Rightarrow c^2=52(c+h).$$
So $\dfrac{CD^2}{AD+CD}=\dfrac{c^2}{h+c}=52$.

**Answer: 52**

dmm-2006-team-04.title: Tangent, arc, tangent
dmm-2006-team-04.body:
The straight line passes through the lake's center, so the shortest path goes along a tangent to the circle, along an arc, then along a tangent to the cheese. The distance from the origin to the center is $13\sqrt2$, so the tangent length is $\sqrt{(13\sqrt2)^2-(5\sqrt2)^2}=\sqrt{288}=12\sqrt2$ (the same from the cheese).

At the center, the angle between the direction to the origin and the tangent point is $\varphi=\arccos\frac{5\sqrt2}{13\sqrt2}=\arccos\frac5{13}$; the same on the cheese side, and the two directions to the origin and to the cheese are opposite. So the arc between the tangent points subtends $\pi-2\varphi=2\arcsin\frac5{13}$ and has length $5\sqrt2\cdot2\arcsin\frac5{13}$. The total is
$$24\sqrt2+10\sqrt2\arcsin\frac5{13}\approx39.52 .$$

**Answer: $24\sqrt2+10\sqrt2\arcsin\frac5{13}\approx 39.52$**

dmm-2006-team-05.title: Newton's identities
dmm-2006-team-05.body:
With $e_1=0$: $e_2=ab+bc+ca=\frac{0-3}2=-\frac32$, $e_3=abc$. Power sums $p_k=a^k+b^k+c^k$ satisfy $p_k=-e_2p_{k-2}+e_3p_{k-3}$ (for $k\ge3$, since $e_1=0$). So
$$p_3=3e_3,\quad p_4=\tfrac32p_2+e_3p_1=\tfrac92,\quad p_5=\tfrac32p_3+e_3p_2=\tfrac92e_3+3e_3=\tfrac{15}2e_3.$$
Hence $\dfrac{p_3p_4}{p_5}=\dfrac{3e_3\cdot\frac92}{\frac{15}2e_3}=\dfrac{27}{15}=\dfrac95$ (valid as $p_5\ne0$ means $e_3\ne0$).

**Answer: $\frac95$**

dmm-2006-team-07.title: Casting out nines
dmm-2006-team-07.body:
$2^{2006}<10^{604}$ has at most $604$ digits, so $f(2^{2006})\le9\cdot604=5436$, so $f(f(2^{2006}))\le4+9+9+9=31$ (e.g. $4999$), and then $f(f(f(2^{2006})))\le11$ (the maximum digit sum of a number up to $31$ is $2+9=11$).

Digit sums preserve residues mod $9$: $2^{2006}\equiv2^{2006\bmod6}=2^2=4\pmod9$ because $2^6\equiv1$. So the result is a positive integer $\le11$ congruent to $4$ mod $9$, hence $4$. (A computer check gives $2^{2006}\to2695\to22\to4$.)

**Answer: 4**

dmm-2006-team-09.title: Area ratios
dmm-2006-team-09.body:
Let $[CNP]=u$ and $[CMP]=v$. Triangles with the same apex $C$ (or $A$) on segments cut by $P$ give
$$\frac{NP}{PB}=\frac{[ANP]}{[APB]}=\frac12=\frac{[CNP]}{[CPB]}=\frac{u}{v+8},\qquad \frac{MP}{PA}=\frac{[PMB]}{[APB]}=\frac45=\frac{[CMP]}{[CPA]}=\frac v{u+5}.$$
So $v=2u-8$ and $5v=4u+20$, giving $u=10$, $v=12$. The whole triangle has area $5+10+8+10+12=45$.

Then $\frac{CN}{CA}=\frac{[BNC]}{[BAC]}=\frac{8+12+10}{45}=\frac23$ and $\frac{CM}{CB}=\frac{[AMC]}{[ABC]}=\frac{5+10+12}{45}=\frac35$. Therefore $[CMN]=\frac23\cdot\frac35\cdot45=18$, and since $R,S$ are the midpoints of $CM,CN$, $[CRS]=\frac14[CMN]=\frac92$.

**Answer: $\frac92$**

dmm-2006-team-10.title: Describe the good numbers
dmm-2006-team-10.body:
Write $k=2^a m$ with $m$ odd. The first press gives $m+1$ (even). Write $m+1=2^s t$ with $s\ge1$, $t$ odd; the second press gives $t+1$. This is a power of $2$ iff $t+1=2^j$, i.e. $t=2^j-1$ ($j\ge1$). So $k$ is good iff $m=2^s(2^j-1)-1$ for some $s,j\ge1$.

Counting the $k\le1023$ by $t=2^j-1$ (that is, by the odd part of $m+1$):
$$\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc}t&1&3&7&15&31&63&127&255&511\\\hline\#k&55&36&28&21&15&10&6&3&1\end{array}$$
for a total of $175$ good values of $k$ (confirmed by running through all $1023$ values). The probability is $\frac{175}{1023}$.

**Answer: $\frac{175}{1023}$**
